attempts.label: DANDI:000021
attempts.entry_title: Long-term orientation adaptation in mouse visual cortex and thalamus (Fritsche et al. 2022)
attempts.summary: The paper's main findings held up in this data. In mouse visual cortex the response to a grating was reduced when a grating of the same orientation came up to 8 trials earlier, decaying with a half-life of about 14 s, while in the thalamus adaptation was limited to the last one or two trials, a result that rests on two reading choices. Adaptation by tuning, its accumulation over trials and the longer trace after static gratings also reproduced. The blank-baseline analysis did not: suppression after an orthogonal grating lasted to 2-back, not only 1-back. A few mice broke the across-mice consistency, and the simulation control failed a criterion that chance noise alone breaks.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Fritsche, Solomon and de Lange (2022) on dandiset 000021, the Allen Brain Observatory Visual Coding Neuropixels sessions of the Brain Observatory 1.1 stimulus set (32 mice). It selects visually responsive units, measures orientation-specific adaptation to drifting and static gratings from 1 to 50 presentations back, fits exponential decay models, compares cortex with thalamus, and repeats the paper's control analyses.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Fritsche et al. (2022) from dandiset 000021

outcomes.statement: The drifting grating analysis rests on 2365 visually responsive neurons in visual cortex and thalamus of 32 mice, with 562 in V1, 140 in LGN and 90 in LP.
outcomes.source: Results, Orientation-specific adaptation in visual cortex and thalamus, paragraph 1; Materials and Methods, Unit exclusion; Figure 1D
outcomes.quote: we analyzed responses from a total of 2365 visually responsive neurons in the visual cortex and thalamus of 32 mice
outcomes.notes: With `noise` units left out and reading O4 a, c, e (rate over the mean plus 1 SD of the blank trials, preferred orientation pooled over directions and temporal frequencies), 2422 units are responsive in the eight regions, V1 580, LGN 142, LP 91, all within tolerance, and all eight named regions have at least 50 units. Without the `noise` filter reading a, d, e also matches (2298; V1 548, LGN 153, LP 92). The other O4 readings give 2214 to 7626 and fail. Units on channels labelled `grey` (122) and `VIS` (71) also pass 50; these labels name no area. With the presentations inside the files' invalid intervals left out (375 drifting in 5 sessions), 2425 units are responsive (V1 585, LGN 140, LP 94), all within tolerance.
deviations: Units the files label `noise` are left out, read as part of the "default quality metrics of the AllenSDK" (Methods, Unit exclusion), whose units table omits them; the unit counts support this reading. The variant without it is shown.
Channels labelled `grey` or `VIS` are not counted as regions; the paper names only areas.

The invalid intervals listed in 13 sessions are not applied; the paper does not mention them. A variant leaves out, for all units of the session, the presentations that overlap them, as current trials and from the responsiveness test (a superset of a per-probe rule); the 1-back ratios move by at most 0.014 (LP) for drifting and 0.004 for static gratings.

outcomes.statement: In V1 the immediate repetition of orientation reduces the early (0 to 100 ms) response to drifting gratings by 17%, a 1-back adaptation ratio of 0.83.
outcomes.source: Results, Orientation-specific adaptation in visual cortex and thalamus, paragraph 1; Figure 1C and 1D
outcomes.quote: Adaptation reduced the response by 17% in V1 (1-back adaptation ratio = 0.83, p = 4e-57, 95% CI [0.81, 0.84])

statistics.test: two-tailed t test of log-transformed adaptation ratios against zero

outcomes.notes: Main reading (O1a pooled per-unit ratio, O2a geometric region value, O3a blanks holding positions, O3c pairs within blocks) gives 0.821 (t interval 0.804 to 0.839), 580 units, t = -18.02, p = 6.0e-58 (paper 4e-57). The four readings with O1a and O2a lie in [0.821, 0.832]; the other 20 readings give 0.848 to 0.931. Per mouse the V1 ratio runs from 0.698 to 0.965.
deviations: The ratio is pooled over current orientations within each unit (O1a); the Methods' "dividing the firing rate of each neuron for repeat by that for orthogonal" (Figure 1D legend) reads most directly this way. All readings are shown.

outcomes.statement: Extrastriate areas show similar 1-back adaptation to drifting gratings, with ratios between 0.80 and 0.88, all significant.
outcomes.source: Results, Orientation-specific adaptation in visual cortex and thalamus, paragraph 1; Figure 1D
outcomes.quote: had a similar impact in higher-level extrastriate visual areas (Fig. 1D; 1-back adaptation ratios between 0.80 and 0.88, all p values < 2e-21, two-sided t tests, corrected for multiple comparisons)

statistics.corrected: multiple comparisons (FDR, Benjamini-Hochberg, per the Methods)
statistics.n: units of LM, AL, RL, PM and AM

outcomes.notes: LM 0.828, AL 0.828, RL 0.876, PM 0.795, AM 0.819, all inside [0.72, 0.968]; largest corrected p 2.0e-24 (paper below 2e-21). Twenty of 24 readings keep all five inside.

outcomes.statement: LGN and LP also show orientation-specific 1-back adaptation to drifting gratings, with ratios of 0.93 and 0.83.
outcomes.source: Results, Orientation-specific adaptation in visual cortex and thalamus, paragraph 1; Figure 1D
outcomes.quote: We also found orientation-specific adaptation in the dorsolateral geniculate nucleus (LGN) of the thalamus (n = 140; 1-back adaptation ratio = 0.93, p = 8e-7, 95% CI [0.91, 0.96]), and the lateral posterior (LP) nucleus of the thalamus (n = 90; 1-back adaptation ratio = 0.83, p = 3e-10, 95% CI [0.79, 0.88])

statistics.test: two-tailed t test of log ratios against zero
two-tailed t test of log ratios against zero

outcomes.notes: LGN 0.935 (0.912 to 0.959), 142 units, p = 6.7e-07 (paper 8e-7); LP 0.833 (0.793 to 0.876), 91 units, p = 1.7e-10 (paper 3e-10). Twenty of 24 readings put both inside the paper's intervals.

outcomes.statement: The 1-back response reduction is consistent across mice, in thalamus and in cortex.
outcomes.source: Figure 1E; Results, Orientation-specific adaptation in visual cortex and thalamus, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: The orientation-specific response reductions for immediate stimulus repetition were highly consistent across mice (Fig. 1E).
outcomes.notes: Cortex, 32 of 32 mice have the orthogonal rate above the repeat rate (sign test p = 4.7e-10), reading (a). Thalamus, 21 of the 23 mice with thalamic units (p = 6.6e-05), so only reading (b) holds there, which the criterion rates as partial. The two mice that fail (a), sessions 744228101 and 754312389, have 4 and 2 thalamic units, with repeat rates 0.36 and 0.97 Hz above orthogonal.

outcomes.statement: In V1, 1-back adaptation is strongest when adaptor and test match the neuron's preferred orientation and weakens for less preferred orientations, a main effect of relative orientation.
outcomes.source: Figure 2D to 2F legend; Materials and Methods, Orientation-specific adaptation to drifting gratings, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: In V1 (D–F, far left columns), adaptation was strongest when adaptor and test stimuli corresponded to the preferred orientation of the neuron and decreased when adapting and testing with less preferred orientations (significant main effect of relative orientation, p = 4e-11)

statistics.test: 3 x 3 mixed ANOVA, main effect of relative adaptor/test orientation
statistics.n: V1 responsive units in three OSI tertiles

outcomes.notes: Mixed ANOVA on log ratios with the 45 degree trials pooled, relative orientation F(2, 998) = 19.97, p = 3.1e-09 (paper 4e-11); the other three readings give p from 9.4e-14 to 2.6e-10. Ratios 0.799 at 0 degrees, 0.875 at 45, 0.927 at 90. 78 of 580 V1 units (96 with averaged 45) are left out for a cell with a zero rate. Every other cortical area also has a significant main effect (p from 5e-11 to 0.027).
deviations: Tertiles are formed on all responsive units of the region before units with a zero-rate cell are left out, so the tertiles are not equal in the ANOVA (194, 192, 116 in V1); the paper does not say how such units were handled. A variant forms the tertiles after the exclusion, and gives the same conclusions.
The mixed ANOVA is computed with the standard split-plot sums of squares and no sphericity correction; the paper names no correction.

outcomes.statement: The dependence of V1 adaptation on relative orientation is strongest in highly orientation-selective neurons (interaction of relative orientation and OSI).
outcomes.source: Figure 2D to 2F legend
outcomes.quote: This relationship was particularly strong in neurons exhibiting high orientation selectivity (significant interaction between relative adaptor/test orientation and orientation selectivity, p = 0.005

statistics.test: 3 x 3 mixed ANOVA, interaction of relative orientation and OSI tertile

outcomes.notes: Interaction F = 3.28, p = 0.011 (log, pooled 45; paper 0.005); 6.3e-07 to 0.018 under the other readings. The spread of ratios over relative orientation is 0.057 (low OSI), 0.125 (medium), 0.248 (high).

outcomes.statement: V1 neurons adapt for all adaptor orientations relative to their preference, except nonpreferred (90 degree) adaptor and test in the most selective units.
outcomes.source: Figure 2D to 2F legend; Results, Orientation-specific adaptation in visual cortex and thalamus, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Nevertheless, there was clear adaptation for all adaptor orientations as indicated by 1-back adaptation ratios consistently smaller than one (all p values < 0.004, corrected for multiple comparisons), except for nonpreferred (90°) adaptor and test stimuli of highly selective units (F, far left column, 90°, p = 0.88).

statistics.about: eight of nine V1 tertile and relative orientation cells
statistics.test: t tests of log ratios against zero
t test of log ratios against zero

outcomes.notes: Pooled 45 degrees, Benjamini-Hochberg over the nine V1 cells, all eight other cells below 1 at corrected p < 0.05 (largest 0.012, medium OSI at 90); high OSI at 90 has ratio 0.993, p = 0.92 (paper 0.88). The same with the family of 72 cells. With Bonferroni 7 of 8 (V1 family) or 6 of 8 (all cells); with averaged 45, 7 of 8 under Benjamini-Hochberg. The 78 units left out are 77 of the 193 high OSI units (a zero rate at 45 or 90 degrees) and 1 medium. With tertiles formed after the exclusion (168, 167, 167), 8 of 8 other cells pass and high OSI at 90 has ratio 0.973, p = 0.62; the main effect (p = 3.3e-09) and interaction (p = 0.033, log) stay significant. On the ratio scale, keeping every high OSI unit with a 90 degree ratio (18 of them 0), the high OSI 90 cell has mean ratio 1.116 over 141 units, p = 0.17 against 1.

outcomes.statement: In LGN and LP, 1-back adaptation does not depend on the adaptor and test orientation relative to preference, nor does that dependence interact with orientation selectivity.
outcomes.source: Figure 2D to 2F legend, two far right columns
outcomes.quote: In thalamic areas (D–F, two far right columns), there was no evidence for a dependence of adaptation on orientation preference (no significant main effects of relative adaptor/test orientation ... LGN, p = 0.28; LP, p = 0.91; no significant interactions between relative adaptor/test orientation and orientation selectivity ... LGN, p = 0.24; LP, p = 0.92)

statistics.about: LGN main effect of relative orientation
LP main effect of relative orientation

outcomes.notes: Log ratios, pooled 45. LGN main effect F = 2.17, p = 0.12 (paper 0.28), interaction F = 1.37, p = 0.25 (0.24); LP F = 0.10, p = 0.91 (0.91), interaction F = 0.19, p = 0.95 (0.92). No reading reaches 0.05; the smallest p is 0.073 (LGN main effect, averaged 45, log); on the ratio scale LGN gives 0.28 and 0.30. Ratios per cell, LGN 0.879 to 0.991, LP 0.795 to 0.863.

outcomes.statement: V1 neurons adapt significantly to drifting gratings seen up to eight presentations (22 s) earlier, despite intervening stimuli.
outcomes.source: Figure 3A; Results, Long-term adaptation in visual cortex but not in thalamus, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Surprisingly, we found that neurons in V1 exhibited significant adaptation effects to stimuli seen up to eight presentations (or 22 s) in the past, despite the presentation of multiple intervening stimuli (Fig. 3A).

statistics.test: two-tailed t tests of log ratios against zero, 1- to 10-back

outcomes.notes: Significant (FDR over n = 1 to 10) at every n from 1 to 8, not at 9 or 10; 8-back ratio 0.984. Seven of 12 readings of O1 and O3 give 8, the four per-orientation arithmetic readings give 2, and one geometric reading 5. In 22 of 32 mice the mean V1 8-back log ratio is below zero.

outcomes.statement: The decay of V1 adaptation over n-back trials is captured by a double exponential with a fast (13.99%, 0.85 trials) and a slow (3.45%, 6.82 trials) component.
outcomes.source: Figure 3A legend; Table 1, row V1; Results, Long-term adaptation in visual cortex but not in thalamus, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: The decay of adaptation over n-back trials was well captured by a double-exponential decay model with a fast- and slow-decaying adaptation component (black dashed line; afast = 13.99%, τfast = 0.85 trials, aslow = 3.45%, τslow = 6.82 trials).
outcomes.notes: All four inside their Table 1 intervals under sign reading (a). Reading (b) fits the same curve with a_slow = -3.76%, outside its interval as a signed value. Fits to the region's mean log ratio (O5a) and to all unit values (O5b) give the same estimates, as every unit has a value at every n. Eight of 12 readings of O1 and O3 put all four inside; the per-orientation arithmetic readings put tau_slow on its bound of 50.
deviations: Fits start from four fixed starting points and keep the lowest residual; the paper does not give its optimizer (a standard choice).

outcomes.statement: Adaptation in this study has a half-life of about 14 s; the paper does not say of which component or area, and it is read here as the slow V1 component for drifting gratings.
outcomes.source: Discussion, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: This half-life is much shorter than the ∼14 s we observed in the current study.
outcomes.notes: tau_slow 6.714 trials x 3 s x ln 2 = 13.96 s (13.97 s with the measured 3.003 s spacing).

outcomes.statement: Taken together, 2- to 8-back stimuli would reduce the V1 response by 19%, more than the 17% reduction from the 1-back stimulus, assuming linear accumulation.
outcomes.source: Results, Long-term adaptation in visual cortex but not in thalamus, paragraph 1; Figure 4A
outcomes.quote: cumulative adaptation to the remote stimulus history outweighed the immediate adaptation effect (17% response reduction to 1-back stimulus vs 19% cumulative response reduction to 2- to 8-back stimuli; Fig. 4)
outcomes.notes: Main reading 1-back 17.88% and cumulative 2- to 8-back 20.36%. The four pooled geometric readings give 18.89 to 20.36% against 16.80 to 17.88%; the arithmetic and per-orientation readings do not match.

outcomes.statement: When two adjacent past stimuli both had the current orientation, the observed adaptation roughly matches that predicted by multiplying the single n-back effects, so adaptation accumulates about linearly.
outcomes.source: Figure 4B legend
outcomes.quote: The empirically observed adaptation effect of two successive stimuli roughly matched the predicted adaptation effect, suggesting that adaptation accumulates approximately linearly in the current setting.
outcomes.notes: With the both-orthogonal baseline (c) the predicted ratio is inside the bootstrapped 95% interval of the observed one for all seven pairs (1-2 observed 0.765, 0.738 to 0.793, predicted 0.754), so pair readings (a) and (b) both hold, under all five seeds. With baseline (d) six of seven pairs hold and pair 1-2 does not (0.788, 0.765 to 0.811), under all five seeds.

outcomes.statement: Adaptation to drifting gratings in the thalamus is limited to the 1-back trial in LGN and the 2-back trial in LP, while cortical areas stay significant for about 6 to 8 trials.
outcomes.source: Results, Long-term adaptation in visual cortex but not in thalamus, paragraph 2; Figure 3B
outcomes.quote: In contrast to adaptation in cortex, adaptation in the thalamus appeared to be limited to the 1-back (LGN) or 2-back trial (LP; Fig. 3B).

statistics.test: t tests of log ratios against zero, 1- to 10-back, per area

outcomes.notes: Counting significant adaptation (corrected p < 0.05 with the ratio below 1), the reading O1a, O3a with pairs across blocks (O3d) meets the criterion, LGN only 1-back, LP to 2, cortex V1 8, LM 8, AL 7, RL 6, PM 7, AM 6. Under the main reading (pairs within blocks) RL stops at 5 and the criterion fails, while LGN and LP still stop at 1 and 2. RL is at the threshold of 6 in the passing reading, and no other of the 12 readings of O1 and O3 passes. Counting significance in either direction, no reading meets the criterion; in the across-blocks reading LGN is also significant at 9-back (ratio 1.024, corrected p = 0.049), so only the partial rule holds there, and in the main reading LP is significant at 3-back (ratio 1.03) while RL stops at 5. With the presentations inside invalid intervals left out, the across-blocks reading still meets the criterion (LGN 1, LP 1, RL 6) and the main reading gives LGN a significant 7-back. With `noise` units kept no reading of O1 and O3 meets the criterion or its partial rule; in the across-blocks reading RL stops at 5 (LGN 1, LP 2), and in the main reading LGN gains a significant 7-back. The question of what Figure 3B's borders mark is for the paper's authors (finding).
deviations: Assumed that "significant adaptation" counts only ratios below 1; a two-tailed test also flags ratios above 1, and the paper does not say whether Figure 3B's borders include those. The Figure 3 legend says of the significant n of panel A that they "still exerted significant adaptation effect", and the Results say adaptation in thalamus "appeared to be limited to the 1-back (LGN) or 2-back trial (LP)"; both speak of adaptation, a ratio below 1. Read two-sided, the outcome would be partially reproduced.
Rests on the `noise` unit filter (see units-responsive-count); with `noise` units kept no reading meets the criterion or its partial rule, as RL stops at 5-back in the across-blocks reading.

outcomes.statement: Adaptation to remote stimuli is stronger in V1 than in LGN (2-, 4- and 9-back) and LP (3-back), even after normalizing to each region's 1-back adaptation.
outcomes.source: Results, Long-term adaptation in visual cortex but not in thalamus, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: adaptation to temporally remote stimuli was significantly stronger in V1 compared with LGN (2-, 4-, and 9-back stimulus, two-sided Welch's unequal variances t test, all p values < 0.02) and LP (3-back stimulus, p = 0.001, corrected for multiple comparisons)

statistics.test: two-sided Welch's unequal variances t test
two-sided Welch's unequal variances t test

outcomes.notes: Over n = 2 to 10 with Benjamini-Hochberg within each pair of regions, V1 is stronger than LGN at exactly 2, 4 and 9 and than LP at 3, both unnormalized (LP also at 4) and normalized by the region's mean 1-back log ratio (b); for reading (b), V1 against LP at 3-back t = 3.77, corrected p = 0.002. Normalizing each unit by its own 1-back log ratio (a) finds none; 38 V1, 11 LGN and 8 LP units have a 1-back log ratio within 0.02 of zero. Over n = 2 to 50, 3 of the four remain unnormalized and 1 under (b).

outcomes.statement: Long-term (4- to 8-back) adaptation is consistent across mice in cortex but not in thalamus.
outcomes.source: Figure 3C; Results, Long-term adaptation in visual cortex but not in thalamus, paragraph 2
outcomes.quote: Mice exhibit consistent long-term adaptation in cortex (right) but not in thalamus (left).
outcomes.notes: 4- to 8-back, cortex 31 of 32 mice (trials pooled; 30 with rates averaged) have orthogonal above repeat, sign test p = 1.5e-08 (reading b); thalamus 14 of 23, p = 0.4, neither reading.

outcomes.statement: Recovery from adaptation to drifting gratings in cortical areas is better fit by a double than a single exponential, in all areas but RL.
outcomes.source: Results, Long-term adaptation in visual cortex but not in thalamus, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: Recovery in cortical visual areas was better explained by double-exponential decay models, with a fast and a slow-decaying adaptation component compared with a single-exponential decay (F tests, all p values < 0.006, except RL, p = 0.072).

statistics.test: F test of nested single- and double-exponential models
F test of nested single- and double-exponential models

outcomes.notes: F tests on the region means, V1 p = 0.0015, LM 0.017, AL 8.0e-05, PM 0.0041, AM 0.011, RL 0.22 (paper RL 0.072); with all unit values, 4.5e-09 to 0.0021 and RL 0.12. Two of the five p values (LM, AM) are above the paper's bound of 0.006.

outcomes.statement: Recovery from adaptation to drifting gratings is slowest in V1 (tau_slow 6.82 trials), and relatively similar in extrastriate areas, whose slow time constants range from 3.12 to 5.52 trials with all 95% CIs overlapping.
outcomes.source: Results, Long-term adaptation in visual cortex but not in thalamus, paragraph 3; Table 1
outcomes.quote: Recovery from adaptation was slowest in V1 with an exponential time constant τslow of 6.82 trials (bootstrapped 95% CI [3.39, 13.50]; Fig. 3A, black dashed line), but was relatively similar for extrastriate areas (τslow ranging from 3.12 to 5.52 trials, all 95% CI intervals overlapping; Table 1).
outcomes.notes: AL, AM, LM, PM and RL tau_slow inside their Table 1 intervals; the six bootstrapped intervals overlap under all five seeds (claim seed, V1 3.79 to 11.59, RL 1.97 to 35.11). V1's tau_slow, 6.71, is the largest. All a_fast, tau_fast and a_slow are inside their intervals. Bootstrap fits on a bound, dropped, 0 to 23 of 1000 per area (RL 23).

outcomes.statement: Recovery in LGN and LP is best described by a single exponential with very short time constants (0.02 and 0.71 trials).
outcomes.source: Results, Long-term adaptation in visual cortex but not in thalamus, paragraph 3; Table 1
outcomes.quote: In contrast, the recovery of adaptation in the thalamus was most parsimoniously captured by a single-exponential decay model (F tests, p = 1 for both LGN and LP), and the time constants of the single-exponential decays were very short (LGN, τfast = 0.02 trials, 95% CI [0.004, 0.63]; LP, τfast = 0.71 trials, 95% CI [0.03, 0.93]).

statistics.about: LGN and LP, double against single exponential

outcomes.notes: F tests not significant, LGN p = 0.81, LP 0.57 (unit values 0.62, 0.19); LGN tau 0.031 and a 6.48%, LP tau 0.712 and a 16.85%, each inside its Table 1 interval. The double fits reach a bound in both. With `noise` units kept the LGN tau falls to 0.000, outside its interval.
deviations: Rests on the `noise` unit filter (see units-responsive-count).

outcomes.statement: Against a blank baseline, both repeated and orthogonal 1-back gratings suppress cortical responses, but only the suppression by repeated orientations persists, up to eight trials back.
outcomes.source: Results, Cortical long-term adaptation is because of suppression following stimulus repetitions; Figure 5
outcomes.quote: Importantly, the suppressive effect of orthogonal orientations decayed quickly and was limited to the 1-back trial, whereas the suppressive effect of repeated stimuli decayed more slowly and remained significant for up to eight trials back (Fig. 5).
outcomes.notes: 2189 cortical units. 1-back repeat over blank 0.757 and orthogonal over blank 0.922, both below 1. Repeat suppression lasts longer, significant by t tests with FDR at 1 to 4 and 7, by the bootstrap interval at 1 to 5, 7 and 9; orthogonal at 1 and 2 (and 4 by the interval). The criterion fails on two parts, under the claim's seed and the four others; orthogonal is still below 1 at 2-back (0.972), and repeat is not significant at 8-back (0.999). Averaged over 100 subsampling draws, repeat is significant to 8-back and orthogonal still at 2-back (0.978). Resampling sessions in place of units (units of a session share one trial subsample), the orthogonal 2-back interval is 0.949 to 0.994 (claim's draw) and 0.961 to 0.996 (100 draws), and repeat 8-back is not below 1 in either (0.960 to 1.002 with 100 draws). The criterion has no partial rule, and the part that fails under every reading and seed is the claim's central contrast, that orthogonal suppression is limited to the 1-back trial. 24 to 30 blank trials per session serve as the 1-back baseline.
deviations: Repeat and orthogonal trials are subsampled per session and per n to the number of n-back blank trials (Methods); the paper does not say whether it drew per session or per n.

outcomes.statement: With brief back-to-back static gratings, orientation repetition reduces the V1 response over 0 to 250 ms, a 1-back ratio of 0.90.
outcomes.source: Results, Long-term adaptation following exposure to brief static gratings, paragraph 1; Figure 6B and 6C
outcomes.quote: In V1 the repetition of stimulus orientation led to a clear reduction of the visual response to the current grating (Fig. 6B, green shaded area; n = 530; adaptation ratio = 0.90, p = 2e-81, 95% CI [0.89, 0.91]).

statistics.test: two-tailed t test of log ratios against zero

outcomes.notes: 0.897 (t interval 0.889 to 0.905), p = 4e-85 (paper 2e-81), 545 V1 units. Eight of 24 readings fall in [0.89, 0.91], all with the pooled ratio.

outcomes.statement: Extrastriate areas show similar 1-back adaptation to static gratings (0.89 to 0.93), and the few responsive LGN and LP neurons also adapt (0.93 and 0.85).
outcomes.source: Results, Long-term adaptation following exposure to brief static gratings, paragraph 1; Figure 6C
outcomes.quote: Very similar adaptation effects were found for extrastriate areas (Fig. 6C; 1-back adaptation ratios between 0.89 and 0.93, all p values < 8e-9, two-sided t tests, corrected for multiple comparisons) ... both LGN and LP exhibited significant adaptation effects (LGN − adaptation ratio = 0.93, p = 0.004, 95% CI [0.93, 0.98]; LP – adaptation ratio = 0.85, p = 0.01, 95% CI [0.85, 0.96])

Although all cortical areas were significantly better fit by a double exponential decay model (F tests, all p values < 1e-5)

attempts.entry_title: In vivo, in vitro and in silico cell classes of mouse V1 (Wei et al. 2023)
attempts.summary: The split of V1 units into fast-spiking (FS) and regular-spiking (RS) clusters on their waveforms held up in this data, and RS units formed the paper's sub-clusters, but FS units did not. Clustering the paper's own published features recovers its sub-clusters, so the gap lies in the features recomputed from the files, which hold only 13 of the paper's 25 sessions. Most sub-cluster differences in visual responses and LFP phase-locking did not reproduce, several weaker effects losing significance with fewer units. Opto-tagged Pvalb units fell in FS and were more symmetric than Sst units, though mainly from a single animal. The mapping onto biophysical models and in vitro cells largely held, tested on the paper's published values.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Wei et al. (2023) on dandiset 000021, the Allen Brain Observatory Visual Coding Neuropixels sessions of the Brain Observatory 1.1 set. From the mean waveforms and spike trains of V1 units it recomputes the one- and multi-channel EAP features and clusters, the firing, drifting-grating and LFP phase-locking properties of the clusters, and the opto-tagged Pvalb and Sst units. The dandiset holds 13 of the paper's 25 wild-type sessions. Claims on the single-cell models and the in vitro cells use the paper's model features, its Source Data and the Allen Cell Types Database.

The depth method follows the criterion, and under the attempt's usual rule, its own reading (c) clusters, the Kruskal-Wallis test gives p = 0.044 (0.011 under reading a, 2.0e-08 under reading b), which meets "Reproduced when it gives p < 0.05". The criterion has no partial clause; the record's reason for figs3b applies equally here, and fig6a-fs1-symmetric and figs4-fs-spread-absent are recorded as reproduced on the same clusters. The outcome is fragile (FS forced to K = 3, a CSD centre not validated, one probe's first sink at 83 ms), and the paper's labels on the same depth give p = 0.36 and the code's centre 0.25 to 0.34; if the six clusters are read as the paper's own, it is not reproduced. The CSD minimum centre (depth_csd_min) is never tested in cell 41. This changes my round-2 view.

paper_notes.statement: The isolation criteria behind the paper's well-isolated units and the code's good flag are not stated. The code's unit tables hold 618 units of the held sessions, of which 15 fail the AllenSDK default filter, while that filter passes 900; every unit of the code's tables has at least 100 spikes in the first 5-min gray screen (fr_5min at least 0.35 Hz), and 270 of the 297 filter-passing units outside the tables have fewer, so the paper appears to require activity during that block as well.

Question for the authors. How were units selected as well-isolated (the good flag of the code's unit tables), how was the layer 4 centre placed from the CSD (the code starts from precomputed depths, which the CSD computed here does not reproduce, and whose centre is the same, 2740 um, on 8 of the 13 probes held), and over which period are the Fig 3a rate, CV and LV taken (neither the presentations nor the whole blocks reproduce the Source Data values)? Which baseline window was used for opto-tagging?

Question for the authors. The phase-locking analysis leaves open the LFP channel, the spikes kept under the 10,000 cap, and what kappa is (the Methods say it ranges from 0 to 1, which a von Mises concentration does not). With the Rayleigh test at p < 0.001 on up to 10,000 spikes, 75% of RS units are phase-locked to theta during the gray screen here, against 4.7% in Fig S7; which spikes and which period were used there?

The code's 3 SD exclusion (ecp_func.outlier_index) uses np.mean and np.std, so a single NaN feature turns the exclusion off for that feature. On this dataset 1/V above is NaN for 14 units of reading (a), and run literally the exclusion keeps a unit at 93.6 ms/mm, which then forms one of the three RS clusters on its own.

The model parameters (conductances) of the 33 models are not public beyond the few columns of the Source Data; the model repository holds one example model. The in vitro features of the Source Data equal those of the Allen Cell Types Database API.

The code's classifiers (ecp_func.classifier after upsampling) upsample the minority classes before the 75/25 split, so copies of a unit fall in training and test. For the random forests of Fig 5c and 5d this inflates the validation accuracy: with permuted RS1 to RS3 labels the procedure scores 61.7% where chance is about 33%, and splitting first gives 97.5% against 98.6% (in vivo) and 85.3% against 93.5% (SP models). For the linear SVM of Fig 4f and 4g the effect is small (53.2% on permuted labels).

entries.description: Tests the findings of Fritsche, Solomon and de Lange (2022) on dandiset 000021, the Allen Brain Observatory Visual Coding Neuropixels sessions of the Brain Observatory 1.1 stimulus set (32 mice). entries.description: Tests the findings of Wei et al. (2023) on dandiset 000021, the Allen Brain Observatory Visual Coding Neuropixels sessions of the Brain Observatory 1.1 set.
